title: Spasticity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Spasticity is an upper motor neuron disorder characterized by velocity-dependent increased muscle tone and exaggerated stretch reflexes resulting from loss of inhibitory supraspinal control. Central nervous system injury affecting corticospinal pathways commonly underlies this condition, including stroke, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy, traumatic brain injury, and multiple sclerosis. Clinical severity ranges from mild hypertonia to profound rigidity with joint immobility. Complications include pain, impaired hygiene, contractures, pressure ulcers, subluxation, heterotopic ossification, and functional decline. In select cases, increased tone may facilitate weight-bearing or ambulation. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by structured tone assessment, and prognosis depends on etiology and timely intervention.

title: Spasticity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity strengthens clinician competence in evaluating and managing spasticity across diverse neurologic conditions. Participants review etiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, and evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, including rehabilitation, pharmacologic therapy, focal injections, and surgical options for refractory cases. Emphasis is placed on early recognition and individualized treatment planning. Collaboration with an interprofessional team that includes rehabilitation specialists, nursing professionals, pharmacists, and therapists enhances coordinated care, reduces complications, and optimizes functional outcomes and quality of life for affected individuals.

title: Spasticity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Determine the etiology of spasticity based on clinical features and relevant diagnostic findings. Implement evidence-based, individualized approaches for managing spasticity and preventing its possible sequelae. Improve awareness of spasticity among patients and their families to promote understanding of its impact on quality of life, participation in care, and timely intervention. Collaborate with all members of the interprofessional team, including specialists such as neurologists, internists, and rehabilitation clinicians, to provide efficient, comprehensive, and coordinated care for individuals experiencing spasticity. title: Spasticity -- Introduction
content: Spasticity is a motor disorder characterized by a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone or tonic stretch reflexes associated with hypertonia. [1] Colloquially, this manifestation is referred to as “tightness” or “stiffness.” Clinical presentation varies, ranging from subtle neurological findings to severely increased muscle tone that can result in joint immobility. [2] Spasticity may cause multiple complications, including interference with daily function, hygiene, and comfort, as well as contractures that increase the risk of pressure ulcers and subsequent infections. Additional risks include subluxation or dislocation and heterotopic ossification. [3] In some patients, spasticity may provide functional benefits, allowing ambulation or standing (weight-bearing), which can reduce the risk of osteoporosis, enhance circulation, and improve overall mental health. [4]

title: Spasticity -- Etiology
content: Spasticity is an important positive sign of upper motor neuron syndrome (UMNS), which encompasses motor behaviors resulting from lesions proximal to the α-motor neuron, within the spinal cord or brain. Other positive features of UMNS include exaggerated muscle stretch reflexes and an upgoing or extensor plantar response (positive Babinski sign). Negative features include motor weakness, slowed movement, loss of dexterity, and impaired selective motor control. Upper motor neuron injury causes loss of downstream inhibition and hypersensitivity of spinal reflex arcs. [5] Multiple central nervous system lesions can produce spasticity, including stroke, cerebral palsy, anoxia, traumatic brain injury (TBI), spinal cord injury (SCI), multiple sclerosis, and various neurodegenerative diseases. [6]

title: Spasticity -- Epidemiology
content: Of the diseases mentioned, spasticity affects approximately 35% of patients with stroke, more than 90% of individuals with cerebral palsy, and about 50% of patients with TBI. This muscle tone abnormality also occurs in 40% of patients with SCI and between 37% and 78% of individuals with multiple sclerosis. [7]

title: Spasticity -- Pathophysiology
content: Although the precise mechanisms underlying spasticity have not been fully elucidated, several key factors have been identified. These factors include abnormal intraspinal processing of afferent signals, loss of descending supraspinal inhibitory control over spinal reflexes, including diminished inhibitory control of the corticospinal tract, and increased excitability of motor neurons. [8] The stretch reflex, also known as the myotatic reflex, is a monosynaptic reflex triggered by passive stretching of the muscle. Muscle spindles—fusiform-shaped sensory receptors within the muscle belly—detect changes in muscle length and the velocity of elongation. Group Ia afferent fibers, which transmit signals more rapidly than group II fibers, carry both length- and velocity-dependent information and serve as the primary afferents in the myotatic reflex. Action potentials generated in the Ia afferents travel toward the spinal cord, passing through the dorsal root ganglion, where the cell body resides, and enter the spinal cord via the dorsal roots at the corresponding spinal level.

title: Spasticity -- Pathophysiology
content: The Ia afferent splits within the spinal cord. One branch projects directly to the ipsilateral ventral horn, where it synapses with an α-motor neuron. The other branch synapses with an inhibitory interneuron. Efferent signals from the activated α-motor neuron cause contraction of the agonist muscle. Simultaneously, inhibitory interneurons suppress activity of the antagonist muscle’s motor neurons, preventing its contraction and facilitating coordinated movement. γ-motor neurons enhance muscle spindle sensitivity, fine-tuning the stretch reflex’s responsiveness. [9]

title: Spasticity -- Pathophysiology
content: Central nervous system lesions disrupt this finely balanced system. The result is a velocity-dependent exaggeration of the stretch reflex, a hallmark feature of spasticity. Two major descending systems from the brainstem modulate stretch reflex excitability: the dorsal reticulospinal tract, originating in the medullary reticular formation, provides inhibitory input, whereas the medial reticulospinal tract, originating in the pontine reticular formation, and the vestibulospinal tract exert excitatory influence on spinal reflex circuits. [10] In addition to neural mechanisms underlying spasticity, including hyperexcitability of stretch reflex pathways and impaired inhibitory control, clinical presentation may be influenced by secondary changes in the mechanical properties of muscles and tendons following UMN lesions. [11] Peripheral adaptations can exacerbate motor impairments and limit functional recovery.

title: Spasticity -- Pathophysiology
content: Common mechanical alterations include reduced tendon compliance, increased passive muscle stiffness, and changes in extracellular matrix composition. Prolonged immobilization or disuse of muscles in shortened positions reduces the number of sarcomeres arranged in series. This structural adaptation allows the muscle to accommodate the persistently shortened length, but it also increases resistance to stretching and limits the muscle’s extensibility and range of motion. Neurogenic and biomechanical factors together produce the complex clinical picture of spasticity observed in patients with UMNS, emphasizing the importance of addressing both neural and structural components in therapeutic interventions.

title: Spasticity -- Histopathology
content: Chronic spasticity has been associated with increased extracellular matrix (ECM) thickness that supports and surrounds muscle fibers, including the endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium. Key contributing factors in this process, besides increased collagen deposition, include the accumulation of hyaluronan—a nonsulfated, high-molecular-weight glycosaminoglycan within the muscle ECM. Hyaluronan influences the viscoelastic properties of the ECM, increasing resistance to deformation, particularly at high strain rates over short time intervals; reducing smooth muscle fiber contraction; strengthening fiber adhesion; and elevating passive stiffness. [12] This heightened resistance to passive stretch is further compounded by structural changes in muscle architecture, including alterations in muscle fibers, collagen content, and tendon properties.

title: Spasticity -- History and Physical
content: A patient may present with new-onset spasticity after suffering a stroke, SCI, or TBI. Alternatively, individuals with a prior diagnosis of multiple sclerosis or cerebral palsy may present with new or worsening preexisting spasticity. On physical examination, hallmark findings include increased muscle tone in the shoulder adductors, elbow flexors, wrist and finger flexors, and forearm pronators. [13] A characteristic finding in the hand is the “thumb in palm” deformity, in which excessive thumb adduction and finger flexion produce a clenched fist with the fingers wrapping around the thumb. In the lower extremities, increased tone is most prominent in the hip adductors, knee flexors and extensors, and ankle plantar flexors and inverters. Spasticity involving the extensor hallucis longus or long toe flexors may cause difficulty with footwear.

title: Spasticity -- History and Physical
content: Clasp-knife rigidity is the typical finding of spasticity on physical examination. Resistance progressively increases until the muscle suddenly yields to the stretch during passive muscle movement. The degree of resistance is velocity-dependent—faster passive movement produces greater resistance to stretch or elongation.

title: Spasticity -- History and Physical
content: Additional physical examination findings include clonus, spastic cocontractions, and spastic dystonia. Clonus consists of alternating contraction and relaxation of agonist and antagonist muscles due to exaggerated stretch reflexes. Spastic cocontractions are abnormal antagonist contractions occurring during voluntary agonist effort. Spastic dystonia is a persistent muscle contraction at rest, producing a constant clinical posture that is highly sensitive to stretch.

title: Spasticity -- History and Physical
content: Spasticity is frequently assessed using the modified Ashworth scale, which ranges from 0 to 4. Other commonly used measures include the Tardieu scale and the Penn Spasm Frequency Scale. [14] The modified Ashworth scale provides a standardized method for grading spasticity based on resistance to passive movement. The categories are as follows: 0: No increase in muscle tone 1: Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested as a catch and release or minimal resistance at the end of the range of motion (ROM) 1+: Slight increase in muscle tone, with a catch followed by resistance through less than half of the ROM 2: More marked increase in muscle tone through most of the ROM, but the affected part remains easily movable 3: Considerable increase in muscle tone, making passive movement difficult throughout most of the ROM 4: Affected part is rigid in flexion or extension

content: The Tardieu scale provides a systematic method to assess spasticity by evaluating muscle response to passive stretch at varying velocities and quantifying both resistance and joint angles. Classification is as follows: Velocity of stretch: V1: Stretch as slowly as possible V2: Stretch at a speed matching the natural drop of the limb under gravity V3: Stretch as fast as possible Muscle reaction: 0: No resistance through passive movement 1: Slight resistance 2: More marked resistance, easily overcome 3: Strong resistance, difficult to overcome 4: Very strong resistance, almost immobile 5: Joint is immobile Spasticity angle: R1: Angle of catch at velocity V2 or V3 R2: Full passive ROM at V1 (muscle at rest) The Penn Spasm Frequency Scale quantifies the frequency and severity of muscle spasms, providing an objective measure for clinical evaluation and spasticity monitoring. title: Spasticity -- History and Physical
content: 0: No spasms 1: Spasms only elicited through vigorous sensory or motor stimulation; no spontaneous spasms 2: Occasional spontaneous spasms and easily induced spasms, occurring less than once per hour 3: Spasms occurring 1 to 10 times per hour 4: Spasms occurring more than 10 times per hour

title: Spasticity -- History and Physical
content: The modified Ashworth scale is the most commonly used clinical tool for grading spasticity due to its simplicity and widespread validation. [15] Combining this assessment method with scales such as the Tardieu or Penn scales can provide complementary information on velocity-dependent responses and spasm frequency, but may prolong assessment time.

title: Spasticity -- Evaluation
content: Clinicians may encounter a patient with new-onset spasticity as an initial manifestation of an underlying neurologic disorder, or a preexisting spasticity that has worsened due to progression of a known chronic condition or an aggravating factor. Evaluation of new spasticity requires a detailed history, including symptom onset and progression, motor weakness, altered sensation, pain, bladder and bowel function, and sexual function. A complete history should also include family history, travel history, diet, and any evidence of immunocompromise. Physical examination should consist of a neurological assessment of muscle tone, motor power, reflexes, and sensation.

title: Spasticity -- Evaluation
content: Evaluation should focus on potential triggers, disease progression, and the emergence of a new disorder in patients presenting with worsening chronic spasticity, which is a more frequent reason for consultation than new-onset spasticity. Common triggers include skin lesions such as ulcers, ingrown toenails, and boils; visceral issues, including constipation, urinary tract infections, and calculi; drug-related causes, such as rapid withdrawal of antispasmodic agents; and device-related factors, including poor seating, ill-fitting orthotics, or an intrathecal baclofen pump malfunction. Additional contributors may include other noxious stimuli, such as infections, injuries, deep vein thrombosis, and stress.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment planning for spasticity requires consideration of etiology, timing of onset, medical comorbidities, the patient’s support system, and overall management goals. Therapeutic interventions generally follow a stepwise approach, beginning with conservative measures and progressing to more invasive surgical procedures as needed. Prior to initiating treatment, clinicians must determine whether the patient’s spasticity warrants intervention. Overtreatment may interfere with activities of daily living or instrumental activities of daily living, increase fall risk, and adversely affect the patient’s therapy program. [16]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management
content: Initial treatment of spasticity involves identifying and avoiding noxious stimuli, including infection, pain, deep vein thrombosis, heterotopic ossification, pressure ulcers, urinary retention or stones, and ingrown toenails. Physical modalities and therapeutics are often implemented next. Measures include stretching, splinting, serial casting, heat and cold therapy, direct tendon pressure, functional electrical stimulation, vibration, and biofeedback. [17] Although transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation has demonstrated safety and tolerability in patients with SCI, evidence for its effectiveness in spasticity remains limited, and further research is needed to clarify its neuromodulatory effects. [18]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Pharmacological Agents
content: Pharmacotherapy offers several options approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), including baclofen, tizanidine, dantrolene, and diazepam. Systemic agents may relieve mild-to-moderate spasticity, particularly in cases secondary to SCI or multiple sclerosis. These drugs reduce tone and pain but have not been shown to produce significant functional improvement.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Baclofen
content: Baclofen functions as a γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) agonist at GABA receptors, increasing inhibitory effects within the reflex pathway. [19] Activation of presynaptic GABA receptors reduces calcium influx, suppressing the release of excitatory neurotransmitters from the presynaptic axon. Postsynaptic GABA receptor activation increases potassium efflux and maintains membrane polarization, making depolarization of the postsynaptic cell more difficult and diminishing the effect of excitatory neurotransmitters. This reduction in neuronal excitability decreases input to muscle fibers and reduces muscle spindle sensitivity. [20]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Baclofen
content: Common adverse effects include sedation and drowsiness, which may improve with tolerance over time. Others include lowered seizure threshold, muscle weakness, gastrointestinal symptoms, tremors, insomnia, and confusion. [21] Baclofen is the drug of choice for spinal forms of spasticity and multiple sclerosis, and it is also used for TBI-induced spasticity. Sudden withdrawal can precipitate seizures, hallucinations, rebound spasticity with fever, renal failure, and death, necessitating a slow taper.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Baclofen
content: Baclofen is primarily metabolized by the kidneys, so dose adjustment is required in patients with renal disease. Transitioning from oral to intrathecal administration may precipitate withdrawal due to lower cerebral concentrations. Baclofen may theoretically interfere with recovery following TBI. Typical dosing begins at 5 mg 2 to 3 times daily, increasing by 5 mg every 3 to 5 days, up to the FDA-recommended maximum of 80 mg/day, though higher doses have been tolerated in some reports. [22]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Tizanidine
content: Tizanidine is an α-2 adrenergic agonist chemically related to clonidine. The mechanism of action of this drug involves enhancing presynaptic inhibition of the spinal reflex. Adverse effects include sedation and drowsiness in up to 50% of patients, liver injury, hypotension, dry mouth, bradycardia, and dizziness. Clinical trials have demonstrated efficacy comparable to that of oral baclofen or diazepam, with improved overall tolerability. [23]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Tizanidine
content: Tizanidine requires precautions due to hepatic metabolism, necessitating frequent monitoring of liver function tests. The drug's short half-life necessitates multiple daily dosing. Concurrent use with intravenous ciprofloxacin is contraindicated because of cytochrome P450 inhibition. Initial dosing begins at 2 to 4 mg/day, typically at bedtime, and may be gradually titrated in both dose and frequency to a maximum of 36 mg/day, divided 3 to 4 times daily, depending on patient tolerance. [24]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Dantrolene sodium
content: Dantrolene sodium is unique among spasticity treatments because it acts peripherally at the muscle level by blocking calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. [25] This action reduces the contraction strength of extrafusal muscle fibers and decreases muscle spindle sensitivity, with minimal effects on smooth or cardiac muscle. Hepatotoxicity is a notable adverse effect that occurs in approximately 1% of patients. The highest risk occurs in women older than 30 who have received higher doses for more than 2 months. Liver toxicity may progress to hepatonecrosis, necessitating close monitoring of liver function tests. Additional adverse effects include drowsiness, sedation, weakness, fatigue, paresthesia, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Dantrolene sodium
content: Dantrolene is preferred for spasticities of cerebral origin, such as cerebral palsy or head injury, but its use is limited in SCI and multiple sclerosis due to associated muscle weakness. The drug is also indicated for malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and hyperthermia resulting from baclofen withdrawal. Dosing begins at 25 mg twice daily and may be titrated up to 400 mg daily, divided into 2 or 3 doses.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Diazepam
content: Diazepam potentiates GABAergic transmission at GABA receptors, leading to membrane hyperpolarization and decreased neuronal firing. The net effect is increased presynaptic inhibition and reduced reflex activity. Diazepam is the most sedating among antispasmodic agents. Additional adverse effects include memory impairment and decreased rapid eye movement sleep. Diazepam has demonstrated efficacy for spasticity associated with multiple sclerosis and SCI, but is often unsuitable for individuals with TBI due to its cognitive side effects. [26]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Diazepam
content: Diazepam undergoes hepatic metabolism, and clearance may be affected by concurrent use of other hepatically metabolized agents. The drug's active metabolites contribute to a long half-life. Concomitant use with alcohol may result in significant central nervous system depression. Overdose may be treated with flumazenil, and withdrawal symptoms may occur if the drug is discontinued abruptly. [27] Initial dosing typically begins at 4 mg at bedtime or 2 mg twice daily. The dose may be titrated up to 60 mg per day, depending on patient tolerance.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemodenervation with Botulinum Toxin
content: This modality is an effective treatment for many patients with spasticity. The FDA has approved 3 type A toxins—onabotulinumtoxin A, incobotulinumtoxin A, and abobotulinumtoxin A—and a type B toxin, rimabotulinumtoxin B. [28] Onabotulinumtoxin A is approved for both upper and lower limb spasticity, while incobotulinumtoxin A is approved for upper limb spasticity.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemodenervation with Botulinum Toxin
content: All serotypes act at the neuromuscular junction by blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release. The toxin is internalized by the nerve terminal, affecting the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor complex and its components: synaptobrevin, synaptosomal-associated protein of 25 kDa (SNAP-25), and syntaxin. Botulinum toxin consists of a heavy and a light chain. The light chain enters the host cell cytoplasm and cleaves SNAP-25, preventing vesicle fusion and exocytosis of acetylcholine-containing vesicles, resulting in chemical denervation.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemodenervation with Botulinum Toxin
content: Contraindications include known sensitivity or infection at the planned injection site. Caution is advised when concurrent aminoglycoside or spectinomycin therapy is used. Patients with underlying neuromuscular disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, and peripheral motor neuropathic disease, are at increased risk of severe reactions, including respiratory depression or dysphagia.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemodenervation with Botulinum Toxin
content: Localization of the target muscle may be performed with electrical stimulation, electromyography, or ultrasound. [29] Dose-dependent effects are observed, with higher toxin loads per muscle producing greater weakness. Onabotulinumtoxin A is typically administered in doses of 25 to 200 units per muscle, depending on muscle size, function, patient weight, and the severity of spasticity.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemodenervation with Botulinum Toxin
content: Onset of action occurs within 24 to 72 hours, with peak effect at 4 to 6 weeks. Clinical duration is approximately 3 months, following the “rule of 3s”: 3 days for the initial effect, 3 weeks for the peak effect, and 3 months of duration. Adverse effects are generally mild and include weakness in adjacent muscles, hematoma, local bruising or swelling, flu-like symptoms, transient dysphagia after cervical injection, and injection site pain. [30] [31]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemodenervation with Botulinum Toxin
content: In addition to oral agents and botulinum toxin injections, spasticity may be managed with interventions such as diagnostic nerve blocks, chemical neurolysis, motor point blocks, selective dorsal rhizotomy, selective neurotomy, and intrathecal baclofen therapy. [32] These procedures reduce muscle tone, although functional improvement is not guaranteed in all cases. Such techniques are typically employed when focal spasticity is documented or systemic effects of oral agents are prohibitive at therapeutic doses. These interventions may decrease muscle tone and improve functional outcomes.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Diagnostic Nerve Blocks
content: Perineural injection of a local anesthetic, typically performed with electrostimulation guidance, can block nerve conduction for several hours. This transient reduction in spasticity allows assessment of functional change and helps guide planning for more durable interventions, including chemoneurolysis, botulinum toxin injection, and surgical procedures. Observation of the temporary response provides insight into the potential benefits of longer-lasting treatments. Local anesthetics act by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels along the axon, preventing depolarization and interrupting action potential propagation. Injection through skin that is infected or cannot be adequately cleansed is contraindicated. Commonly used agents include lidocaine and bupivacaine.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemoneurolysis
content: Chemical neurolytic agents produce effects lasting from months to years by inducing demyelination and axonal destruction through protein denaturation and axonal necrosis. [33] Administration is typically performed using electrostimulation or electromyography guidance. Commonly used agents include phenol and ethyl alcohol.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemoneurolysis
content: Phenol is generally administered at concentrations ranging from 2% to 7%. Lower concentrations primarily cause demyelination, resulting in a transient anesthetic effect with minimal axonolysis. Higher concentrations exert neurolytic effects by destroying axons, with clinical response lasting longer than 6 months. Ethyl alcohol is administered at concentrations of 45% to 100% to achieve neurolysis. Compared with phenol, ethyl alcohol is used less frequently and is associated with lower toxicity.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Chemoneurolysis
content: A common adverse effect of chemoneurolysis is dysesthesia, defined as pain within the sensory distribution of the targeted nerve. Reported incidence ranges from 10% to 30%, with symptom duration lasting weeks to months. Additional adverse effects include muscle weakness, which may be permanent; transient intramuscular swelling or nodule formation; deep vein thrombosis; sprains; and skin sloughing, which occurs more frequently with phenol injections. Intravascular injection of phenol may result in severe systemic reactions, including convulsions, central nervous system depression, and cardiovascular failure. Accordingly, administered doses remain well below the lethal threshold of 8.5 g and are typically limited to 20 to 30 mL of a 5% solution. Ethyl alcohol produces minimal systemic effects when injected intravenously. [34]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Intrathecal Baclofen Pump
content: Another management option is ITB pump therapy. This approach enables direct delivery of baclofen into the cerebrospinal fluid within the intrathecal space. Intrathecal administration achieves high drug concentrations in the spinal cord while reducing central nervous system adverse effects associated with high oral doses, providing an approximate 100:1 concentration advantage over oral administration. [35]

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Intrathecal Baclofen Pump
content: The system consists of a pump and reservoir implanted subcutaneously within the abdominal wall and a catheter positioned in the intrathecal space. A programmable, battery-powered pump stores and delivers baclofen according to a preset electronic schedule. Reservoir refilling is performed intermittently via transcutaneous injection, with refill intervals determined by infusion rate and reservoir capacity. Dose adjustments can be made at any time using an electronic programmer. Integrated alarm functions alert the patient, caregiver, and clinician to low reservoir volume or device malfunction.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Intrathecal Baclofen Pump
content: Symptoms of baclofen overdose include hypotonia or severe weakness, somnolence, nausea and vomiting, hypotension, respiratory depression, and seizures. Baclofen withdrawal may manifest as fever, nausea, hyperthermia, dizziness, insomnia, pruritus, hallucinations, altered mental status, and exaggerated rebound spasticity. Intrathecal  baclofen pump therapy is indicated for patients with generalized spasticity who do not tolerate or respond adequately to conservative treatments, including oral medications and nerve blocks. [36] Careful assessment of the functional utility of spasticity remains essential prior to intervention.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Intrathecal Baclofen Pump
content: Before pump implantation, candidates must undergo screening trials using a single intrathecal bolus or continuous infusion via a percutaneous catheter. Multiple trials with escalating doses may be required to establish clinical benefit. Demonstration of a meaningful reduction in tone or spasm frequency supports candidacy for pump placement. Initial infusion dosing is commonly calculated by doubling the effective screening dose to determine the first 24-hour infusion rate. Intrathecal baclofen pump therapy requires strict adherence to follow-up, as regular monitoring and refilling are mandatory, and abrupt withdrawal may be fatal.

title: Spasticity -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Surgical intervention is the most invasive management option for spasticity. Available procedures include orthopedic approaches, such as tendon lengthening and tendon transfer procedures, including split anterior tibial tendon transfer, as well as neurosurgical techniques. Neurosurgical options include peripheral nerve sectioning (neurectomy), rhizotomy, neuroablative procedures, and implantation of central electrical stimulators. [37] Epidural spinal cord stimulation has demonstrated potential benefits in reducing spasticity and improving ambulation across several UMN disorders. However, the available evidence remains limited by small sample sizes, methodological heterogeneity, and a lack of high-quality randomized controlled trials. [38]

title: Spasticity -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnoses for spasticity include contractures, rigidity, and catatonia. A contracture is defined as decreased elasticity of a muscle, tendon, ligament, joint capsule, or skin, resulting in increased resistance during passive stretch, similar to spasticity. Unlike spasticity, contractures do not exhibit velocity-dependent changes with movement or limb positioning.

title: Spasticity -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Rigidity is most commonly associated with basal ganglia injuries. This motor abnormality is characterized by high tone that is nonselective, affecting all muscles surrounding a particular joint equally. Similar to contractures, rigidity is unaffected by movement speed and remains constant throughout the range of motion.

title: Spasticity -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric disorder in which patients demonstrate abnormal posturing. Increased muscle tone in catatonia depends on the force applied to the affected muscle. Unlike spasticity, catatonia frequently occurs with additional signs, including stupor, impulsivity, perseveration, staring, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia, and withdrawal.

title: Spasticity -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Human recombinant hyaluronidase has emerged as a promising therapeutic option for treating spasticity. Hyaluronan, a high-molecular-weight glycosaminoglycan (GAG), contributes to the viscoelastic properties of the ECM. In individuals with spasticity, elevated hyaluronan concentrations are associated with increased tissue viscosity and reduced muscle pliability, limiting both passive and active range of motion. This accumulation interferes with normal muscle contraction and fiber extensibility, exacerbating functional impairment. Human recombinant hyaluronidase enzymatically hydrolyzes hyaluronan, reducing the GAG's concentration and mitigating the associated decrease in tissue stiffness. Although approved by the FDA for hypodermoclysis (subcutaneous fluid administration), intramuscular use remains off-label. [39]

title: Spasticity -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Several studies' results report that off-label intramuscular injections of human recombinant hyaluronidase can significantly improve muscle flexibility, passive and active range of motion, and functional mobility. [40] These benefits occur without adverse effects commonly seen with conventional spasticity treatments, such as muscle weakness from oral antispasmodics or chemodenervation techniques, including botulinum toxin or phenol injections. Therapeutic effects have been shown to persist for up to 3 months, indicating the need for periodic readministration to maintain functional gains. [41] Emerging evidence supports the use of human recombinant hyaluronidase as a valuable adjunct or alternative to existing therapies, particularly in cases of refractory spasticity where traditional interventions provide limited benefit.

title: Spasticity -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of spasticity varies considerably between patients. Spasticity that responds well to physical modalities, therapy, or pharmacological interventions may have a favorable symptomatic outcome. In some cases, spasticity may provide functional benefits, such as assisting with ambulation, promoting weight-bearing, maintaining muscle bulk, reducing the risk of deep vein thrombosis, and preventing osteoporosis.

title: Spasticity -- Complications
content: Complications of spasticity can vary in severity. Severe spasticity may interfere with daily function, cause significant discomfort or pain, and impair hygiene and caregiving. These factors can increase the risk of pressure ulcer formation, which may progress to infection and sepsis. Additional complications include bone fractures, subluxation, dislocation, and a heightened risk of heterotopic ossification.

title: Spasticity -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Rehabilitation frequently plays a critical role in managing spasticity. In addition to pharmacological interventions, physical modalities and therapeutic strategies should be applied as indicated. Patient, family, and caregiver involvement is essential to establish and achieve treatment goals. Identification and avoidance of potential noxious stimuli, along with consistent stretching and range-of-motion exercises, are key components of management. [42]

title: Spasticity -- Consultations
content: Referral to specialty services may be considered, depending on the clinical scenario. New-onset spasticity or worsening spasticity without identifiable triggers may warrant consultation with neurology. Consultation with a physiatrist should be considered for patients who have not improved with antispasticity medications or have symptoms that significantly affect posture, mobility, or overall care.

title: Spasticity -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients should be instructed to maintain a daily stretching and range-of-motion program. Families and caregivers should receive education on proper positioning, daily skin inspection, maintaining an adequate and regular bowel and bladder regimen, avoiding noxious stimuli, and recognizing signs of infection and pain.

title: Spasticity -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Spasticity is optimally managed by an interprofessional team, including nurses, pharmacists, and therapists. Treatment planning requires consideration of spasticity etiology, timing of onset, medical comorbidities, the patient’s support system, and overall management goals. Therapeutic interventions generally follow a stepwise approach, beginning with conservative measures and progressing to more invasive surgical procedures as needed. Outcomes in chronic cases are often guarded.
